title: Al-Hujurat, whole
tomorrow: why does a stranger come running from the far end of a city?

cards: Some people knock. Some people sit in the driveway and honk. In the scene that names this surah, people stand outside the private rooms of the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, and call out to him to come out.
They don't wait. They don't knock. They shout through the walls.
The surah says waiting until he came out to them would have been better for them. That's al-Hujurat, the private rooms.
And by its end, this little surah of manners answers a very big question: why are people made different at all?

teach.b: From that doorway the surah reads like a guide to living with people. Don't raise your voices over the Prophet's.

If someone untrustworthy brings you news, "verify it, lest ye smite some folk in ignorance and afterward repent of what ye did." If two groups of believers fight, make peace between them; believers are brothers.
Don't mock another group; they may be better than you.
Don't call each other by insulting nicknames. Avoid much suspicion, don't spy, don't backbite. Here's the detail to tell a friend tonight: verse after verse opens O ye who believe.

teach.h: O YE WHO BELIEVE, THEN O MANKIND.
teach.b: Then, near the end, the address widens to everyone: "O mankind! Lo! We have created you male and female, and have made you nations and tribes that ye may know one another. Lo! the noblest of you, in the sight of Allah, is the best in conduct."
One pair at the root of everybody.
Nations and tribes are real, and the verse keeps them; it doesn't erase anyone's people.
But it gives them a reason: so that you would know one another. Not rank one another. Not wall each other off.
Know. And the only ranking that counts is conduct, which God sees, and we mostly don't. A surah that starts with people shouting through a wall ends with the walls between peoples turned into doors.

how: Al-Hujurat 49:13 is quoted by Muslims in sermons and talks about the equal dignity of people of every nation; the surah's rules on verifying news, nicknames and backbiting are taught as everyday manners.

o: the Private Rooms: surah 49, the surah of manners
the Women: a surah of family and inheritance law
the Gathering: a surah about the Day of Judgment

games.q: the surah of manners — tap the pairs.
p: that ye may know one another

s: the surah is named for the private rooms people shouted outside
after verses to 'ye who believe', it turns to 'O mankind'.
the verse says nations and tribes don't matter
it keeps them, and gives a reason for them: that ye may know one another.

games.q: at the senior picnic, everyone sits with their own group again. a friend wants to mix up the tables. what fits 49:13?
o: leave it: the verse says God made tribes, so stay with yours.
mix them, and tell everyone their backgrounds don't matter at all.
mix with care: let groups stay real, and give people a way to meet.
games.why: the verse keeps nations and tribes, and gives them a purpose: that ye may know one another. not walls, and not erasing anyone.

practice: Close your eyes and bring to mind one person you mostly know by a label: the new kid, the neighbor from somewhere else, the coworker with the accent.
For the sit, just hold them there, and find one real question you'd like to ask them.

wordCard.voice: Al-Hujurat. The private rooms: surah 49, the surah of manners, which ends by turning nations and tribes into a reason to meet.

orig.note: Arabic: the private rooms. surah 49 takes its name from the scene at the Prophet's door.

carryVoice: Keep this one close: know one another, not rank, not wall off, but know. Day done, door open.
